The constraint has moved from building to deciding what to build and getting it adopted.

  • Coding and testing are 25 to 35% of idea-to-launch time. Free code still leaves 15 to 25 of the 50 points needed to halve it.
  • Value leaks at the joins: feedback nobody consolidates, decisions left unwritten, and growing review queues.
  • Six recommendations follow. Part 2 runs end to end, but its quality floors fail (slide 7).

Seven stages, five human gates: agents read, draft and check; people decide.

  • Agents work in every stage. A named person passes each of the five gates, and no agent merges its own work.
  • Each stage hands a typed artefact to the next, and every move is logged.
  • Product ops owns what crosses squads; the platform team keeps the coding harness.

EnableHelp articles, videos, post-call briefsGate 5: comms (product marketing manager)

The factory is a delegation meta-harness: it routes work to people and to coding tools, and passes the human gates. Owning the coding harness is not required.

What I leave alone

  • The coding-agent harness: a second one would split two engineers.
  • Code-review policy: engineering owns it; I supply review-wait data.
  • Squad structure: changing it with tooling would hide which approaches worked.
  • The design system: I only generate mockups on its components.

The platform contract

An intent document plus a factory job, checked against a versioned JSON Schema (draft v1) that both teams own. The job carries references and de-identified text; quotes and account names stay inside the company's private network.

Route each task by the cost of being wrong: Opus orchestrates, cheaper models build, Codex Sol checks.

  • Opus 5.5 splits, routes and checks, and never writes production code. Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Codex Terra build.
  • Codex Sol checks, so the checker is always a different model family from the builder. A person passes every merge.
  • The open stack waits in reserve and routes no tasks until 50 shadow tasks clear the bar the judges must clear.

More: Clef as router and triager, and the open stack's bar

Clef, an open-weight decision model, would answer four typed questions at work-order intake: task class, crown-jewel path, spec clear enough, expected size. Code decides T3, and below its confidence threshold a task routes one class up, never down. Clef Flash is the fallback. This is designed, not built in this demo.

Open modelStatus on 05/11/2026
GLM 5.3Weights public by 28/08/2026, custom licence; the back-pocket builder
DeepSeek V4.1 FlashMIT licence, 17/10/2026 snapshot; a back-pocket checker
Qwen3.8Open weights for the 27B; larger variants are API-only; a back-pocket checker
Qwen 4Not released; named only as the planned next step

A task class moves to the open stack only when, on at least 50 shadow tasks of that class, its first-check pass rate has a Wilson 95% lower bound no more than 5 points below the hosted stack's, and its escaped-defect rate is not higher. Shadow runs replay past work orders with their hidden tests and never touch live code.

Tell the board: halving idea-to-customer time is not plausible within 18 months.

  • On my mid inputs lead time is 79% of today's at month 18. The high case reaches 51%, and AI alone 95%.
  • All 24 inputs are my assumptions, so this is a model output, not a measurement.
  • A 90-day pilot against a control squad starts replacing assumptions with data.

More: what would change the answer, and the monthly tracker
  • Coding speed alone cannot do it. In a study of 40 product managers, a 40% productivity gain moved time to market about 5%.
  • The recommendation changes if pilot decision time halves and release time falls 70%, if acceptance stays below 30% after calibration, or if customers reject bundles.
  • Fund review first if it takes more than 12% of lead time.
  • Each month: load real stage timestamps, run the tracker command, read both lead-time definitions against the 50% target and throughput against +100%, then post one line to the board.

The tracker's current figures are invented demo data: idea-to-customer sits 5% of the way to target. Do not report them to the board as real.

DayWhat runs, and who uses itGo or learning test
30The Signal Engine nightly for a pilot squad; a "what shipped" digest for every squad. All PMs label for a half-day.A pilot PM accepts three of the top 10 in 30 minutes.
60All routes plus sessions; intent-doc handoff for two squads; decision log; metric dictionary v0; a bundle pilot with three large customers.Acceptance above 30%; no pilot customer leaves bundles.
90Intake for three to five squads, depending on staffing; outtake drafts (release notes, help articles, change notices, follow-up briefs).Pilot against control; where the bottleneck moved.
  • The VP Product sponsors it and a pilot squad volunteers. The digest removes status reporting before PMs label anything.
  • My ask is one engineer for 90 days. Without one, day 90 covers three squads, not five.
  • Labelling happens in the Monday review, where the board replaces the weekly feedback meeting. It takes a half-day at day 30, then about 30 minutes a week.
  • Three metrics: weekly active PMs, the share of decisions with a written rationale, and the share of customer-visible changes flagged.

Part 2 runs end to end: raw feedback goes in, a ranked and cited list comes out for the PM.

  • Code checks every quote against the customer's own turn and every number in a brief against a fact sheet.
  • Cheap models handle the volume. A strong model writes only the top 10 briefs, and three judges from another model family check them.
  • It runs today on synthetic data from file exports. Production needs about 14 to 22 more engineer-weeks (an estimate).
More: each step in detail, with the README diagram
StepWhat happens, and with which model
1 CollectSales calls, support tickets, onboarding and account calls and sessions arrive each night. Code keeps the customer's turns and cuts idle session time.
2 FilterClef (Clef Flash as fallback) answers three typed questions: signal, bucket, severity. Small talk is dropped; about 40 dropped items a week go to a PM audit.
3 ExtractQwen3.8 Flash writes the problem and the customer's exact words; code finds those words in the customer's own turn.
4 RankPull in account data from HubSpot, cluster similar problems, match the roadmap and what shipped; a formula ranks them.
5 DecideThe top 10 get a cited brief (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash). Three judges (GLM 5.3) check it. The PM decides on the board; accepting drafts an intent doc and a factory job.

Each Monday a PM opens one ranked list, with the evidence and every check beside each item.

  • The board ranks the problems customers keep raising. Each top-10 item carries a cited brief and its ranking factors.
  • The target is a review of the top 10 in 30 minutes. Accepting an item drafts an intent document and a factory job.
  • The checks show their failures: a brief that fails a number check stays hidden, and no judge is trusted yet (0 of 3).
More: the About tab, and what each tab is for
  • Real: the code, the AI models, the checks and the audit trail. Code verifies every quote against its source and every model call is logged.
  • Simulated: the customers, calls and tickets (30 fictional insurers). In the static snapshot the PM buttons are switched off.
  • Opportunities: the ranked list. Handoffs: the build brief drafted for each accepted item. Pipeline: what each stage kept, dropped and cost. Evals: the run against the planted answers; several checks fail and the tab says so. Audit: every decision and model call, in a log that shows tampering.

Screenshots are from a replay run on synthetic data. Keelwater is fictional.

More: the same run in Phoenix, and what it holds

The run is recorded in Phoenix as 1,250 spans in one trace. Phoenix also holds 4 datasets and 1 experiment. There are no human labels yet, so human and judge verdicts cannot be shown side by side.

Running cost is about USD 0.17 per nightly run at demo volume, from list prices and the recorded token counts.

It runs end to end, but its quality floors fail, and the board says so.

  • Seed 42: recall, noise dropping, bucket accuracy and quote checks hold. Theme recovery (1 of 6) and mean purity (0.54 against 0.75) do not.
  • Held-out seed 43 recovers 0 of 3 themes, stability fails, and no judge is certified (0 of 50 real PM labels per class).
  • I capped the fix at one re-run per seed, so the floors ship as measured on the 05/11/2026 routing.
More: every check against its floor

Floors come from docs/evals.md; PASS and FAIL are each suite's own gates. All data is synthetic, so these measure the pipeline against planted truth, not real customers.

{{RESULTS_TABLES}}

Stability fails: no September opportunity lost its id (0 of 12) and no membership shrank, but 2 planted themes are held by two opportunities of 25% or more each.

More: the judges, and why none is certified
{{JUDGES_TABLE}}

The constructed items never certify a judge. Each judge needs 50 real PM labels per class and a Wilson 95% lower bound before the board trusts it. None has any, so all three read "calibrating". The judge suite passes its own gates: every item judged, no trust without labels.

More: what the re-run changed, and what the verification found
{{EARLIER_TABLE}}
  • Clustering is the limit: average-linkage cosine cannot separate planted themes that share vocabulary. Citation failures come from the brief stage.
  • On the new routing, Qwen3.8 Flash and 27B reason by default and ran out of tokens, so extract runs with reasoning off. Brief and handoff moved to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, because Qwen3.8 Max cannot switch its reasoning off.
  • From a clean clone with no key, the replay printed MATCH in 58 seconds.
  • An adversarial review by Codex Sol, a different family from the Sonnet builders, blocked twice. Fixes came with failing-first tests, and three narrowed items are listed in the README Limits.

AI built most of it; I held the spend limit and every judgement call.

  • Claude did most of the work: Opus orchestrated, Sonnet built 12 of 13 work orders and checked every pull request, and Haiku read and searched.
  • At API prices the build is worth about USD 149 across 628,278,423 measured tokens. I paid for subscriptions I already hold, plus OpenRouter spend of USD 6.67 of the USD 10 limit to 05/11/2026; the work-order reports gave a subtotal of USD 0.51 measured and 1.44 estimated.
  • I overrode four AI recommendations. The AI got two things wrong, and a check caught both.

More: where I trusted it, where I overrode it, what it got wrong
  1. Trusted: mechanical work (scaffolding, schemas, test plumbing) once the tests ran and a separate check passed.
  2. Overrode: open-weight models instead of a paid frontier API, a public repo, a one-day demo build, and keeping a decision model the AI had dismissed.
  3. Wrong, and caught: the AI put a closed-weight, US-hosted decision model into production triage; research found it cannot run inside a private network, so I replaced it. A worker's report said 5 links where the PDF had 4; a separate check caught it after the first check had passed the same commit, and the issue was reopened.
